Odin in Godot

7 · Server-authoritative simulation

4 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Predict-self: your avatar on both timelinesChoosing per object: predict-self and contestedPresentation claimsLag compensationSession features and migration limits

The co-op model gives each player authority over their own avatar: you write your position, everyone else reads it. That works when you trust the other players. The authority accepts their motion, so this policy cannot prevent a modified client from inventing a position.

For contested motion, the server runs the authoritative simulation. A client predicts its own input before the server replies. When an update disagrees, the client restores historical state and reruns subsequent ticks with the correction. Presentation then blends toward that result.

kit/sim implements this simulation lane. It uses the same field declarations and generated callbacks as cooperative replication, with additional input, tick, and history configuration. Each field selects its replication policy, so a game can combine lobby and scoreboard deltas with server-authoritative hitboxes. Presentation still needs to align effects with their visible causes.

Predict-self: your avatar on both timelines#

In the co-op lane your avatar's x, y are gd:"owner": you own them and you stream them. In the sim lane they become predicted state, and the tick that moves them is a plain proc with a tag:

Odin
Fighter :: struct {
	body: psim.Mover,          // x/y/vx/vy — predicted, resimmable
	hp:   i32 `gd:"replicate"`, // authority-owned state on the delta lane
}

@(gd_tick)                     // "predict-self": predict the local fighter; authority judges it
fighter_tick :: proc(self: ^Fighter, input: Fighter_Input) {
	// Read input and write intent. Runs live on the client each simulation
	// tick, re-runs during a resim after a server correction, and runs on
	// the authority. The generated scheduler handles is_host role selection.
}

@(gd_tick) registers the tick procedure. With the session and predicted fields configured, the simulation lane runs it locally and on the authority. It delivers typed input, retains history, and applies corrections; gameplay code does not send the input packets directly.

Choosing per object: predict-self and contested#

A remote avatar renders in the past (see timelines). Choose which objects to predict locally and which to display from received authority history:

  • Predict-self: the default @(gd_tick). Predict only your fighter; display the opponent from accepted history an interp-delay behind. Use this for interactions judged against the displayed opponent, such as hitscan shots and parry windows. Quickdraw uses this model.
  • Contested: @(gd_tick = "contested"). For a shared object both players hit: a ball, a flag, or a bomb. Marking it contested makes every peer predict it, so local simulation can respond to contact before a round trip. The server remains authoritative. A disagreement restores and replays the predicted state, while presentation blends toward the corrected result.

Three soccer examples demonstrate different prediction and presentation models:

example model the ball is…
examples/slopball co-op owned by the last toucher; peer-authoritative
examples/speedball predict-world predicted on every peer along with avatars; one timeline with blended corrections
examples/claimball predict-self + claim only your avatar predicted; the ball predicted and claimed

Presentation claims#

claimball combines predict-self with a contested ball. The local peer predicts the ball while displaying the opponent from delayed authority history. Always drawing the predicted ball can therefore show an opponent's shot an interp-delay before the opponent visibly kicks it.

A presentation claim chooses the local predicted view while the local player drives the ball. It does not transfer network authority. Update it continuously from the local influence on the ball:

Odin
// In the world pass, claim each tick while the local fighter influences the ball:
if ksim.lane_live(&g.lane) {          // presentation — live pass only, never a resim
	if my_kicker_in_reach || ball_still_fast_from_my_kick {
		ksim.lane_claim(&g.lane, ball.net_id)   // draw from the local predicted pose
	}
}

While claimed, the ball draws from local prediction to respond to the local player's influence. Without a claim, it draws from watched history to align with the opponent's delayed avatar. When local influence ends, the claim decays over a quarter second and blends toward the watched view.

Keep the claim while the ball remains fast from the local kick, even after it moves far from the player. Releasing it based only on distance blends toward the older watched position and can visibly pull the ball backward mid-flight. Release when the ball slows: the position gap between the timelines is then smaller, reducing the visible correction during the handoff.

Lag compensation#

For a hitscan shot, the server's current target position may differ from what the shooter saw. The lane retains recent entity history so the authority can temporarily rewind targets to the shooter's view for the hit test:

Odin
judged := ksim.lane_rewound_begin(&g.lane, shooter) // rewind other entities with history
g.hit = trace_shot(g)                               // back to the shooter's view
ksim.lane_rewound_end(&g.lane)

Call this pair on the authority inside its simulation step. Begin and end must occur in the same frame, must not nest, and must not surround changes to the lane's tracked entity set. The end call restores the live state.

Session features and migration limits#

Reconnects, drop-in joins, saves, wire-version compatibility checks, and transports use the same session. A game can keep cooperative lobby/chat state and authoritative hitboxes together. Live host migration is supported only for the cooperative lane; boot_migration requires that no simulation lane is installed. A simulation save can resume under a restarted authority, with fresh lane history; see the save contract.

Run it:

Code
nix develop --command bash -c 'bash examples/claimball/native_run.sh'  # CLAIMBALL_NATIVE_OK

The test runs three headless processes at 240ms round-trip. A striker predicts and claims the ball through its flight to the goal, presenting from the striker's timeline with claim near 1. A watcher that never touches it uses the watched view with claim 0. These checks exercise the two presentation choices for that scenario.

See kit/sim for simulation setup and APIs, and timelines for choosing a replication and authority policy for each field.
